title: Share Bench
context: Grade 4, the first working topic of the division chapter, and the one every later topic leans on. An adult sees counters being shared out, which a class can do with real counters. What is actually being settled is the language and the limits: which of the four numbers is which, why a leftover can never be as big as the divisor, and which of the chapter's rules hold for every number. Two of those rules are printed with the word always and no condition, and zero divided by zero would then get three answers: one, zero and not possible. Only the last is right, so this tool states the other two for a divisor other than zero.

writeup.why: Share a heap equally onto plates, name the four numbers that come out of it, and find out which sharings cannot be done at all.
writeup.look: A tray of counters at the left, a row of plates along the middle with a leftover dish beside them, and four name tags waiting at the side.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Share Bench' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the rounds dealt against the counters the heap began with, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each round lands on the plates, which makes it one plate's share, and the second fixed at the size of the heap. On the first phase it carries the rows and the counters in a row instead. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The tray occupies 320 by 300 at 64,220, its counters in deep blue laid in rows of ten, at most ninety-nine of them, none overlapping. The plate dial sits under it, 320 by 56 at 64,532, running from none upwards, and the four name tags lie below that, each 150 by 44, at 64,604, 234,604, 64,660 and 234,660, reading dividend, divisor, quotient and remainder. The fact card runs across the top of the bench, 660 by 110 at 420,210, holding the same counters as equal rows with the multiplication written under them; turning it swings the rows round a quarter turn so that rows become columns, and writes one division for each reading. The plate rail stands under the card, 520 by 280 at 420,334, laying out whatever number of plates the dial sets in rows of ten, in amber, every plate on one deal the same size and none overlapping, so twelve plates stand in two rows and thirty-four in four. Deal a round lifts exactly as many counters out of the tray as there are plates and puts one on each at the same moment, and one plate's share is printed under each plate in green as it settles. The leftover dish stands apart from the plates, 150 by 130 at 956,334, taking in vermilion what cannot go round; its lid stays open while it holds as many counters as there are plates, and then every plate that could take one more lights. The rule bay sits under the dish, 150 by 150 at 956,478, four keys reading one plate, as many plates as counters, an empty tray and no plates at all. With no plates the deal control stays unlit and the caption says there is nowhere to put a share; no number is drawn anywhere on the stage for it. The check bar runs along the foot, 686 by 70 at 420,640, and multiplies the plates by one plate's share, adds the dish, and builds the heap again in rows of ten beside the tray. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a count is asked for. On the second phase a word pad sits over it with the four names, dividend, divisor, quotient and remainder, and on the fourth it carries a key reading not possible, so a division by zero is answered by press and never with a number. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the dividend, the whole being shared and any total, is deep blue; the divisor, and the plates, groups or envelopes it makes, is amber; the quotient and each equal share are green; what is left over, at one step or at the end, is vermilion; a multiple of the divisor, tried on a ladder or taken away as a chunk, is rose; and a zero written in the quotient because the number was smaller than the divisor is grey. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because what is left over is told by the dish or the slot it sits in, a quotient digit by the row it sits in, and a multiple by the rung or the column that holds it, before any of them is told by a colour, and every rule, bracket, cell edge and guide line is near-black. Grey never means faint: a zero in the quotient is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. The leftover dish is never inside a plate and never under one. It stands apart at full strength, and it keeps its lid open until what it holds is smaller than the number of plates, because a leftover that could still go round is not a remainder yet.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last heap the child shared, its plates and leftover dish still drawn, with the four name tags where the child dropped them and the check written underneath.

phases.win: both division facts settle under the fact card, one for each number that was multiplied
phases.does: reads the rows one way and writes a division, then turns the card and writes the other
phases.goal: a multiplication fact with no zero in it gives two division facts, one for each number that was multiplied
phases.says: Read the rows one way. Now turn the card. What does each way divide by?
phases.check: Away from the screen: lay out four rows of six counters, then write both divisions they show.
phases.feels: one set of rows, read from two sides, and each side divides by a different number
phases.hands: Lay out counters in four rows of six on a desk. Read them as four rows of six, then walk round to the other side of the desk and read the same counters as six rows of four. Write one division from each side, and ask what number each one divided by. Then take six away from the whole heap again and again, counting the takes, and ask which of the two divisions the number of takes matches.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what is the product on the card? Second rung, the phase's: how many are in each row, and how many rows are there? Third rung: the card is cut to two rows of three and the child writes both divisions from it before the larger card comes back. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the recap's worked model turns six fifteens into ninety divided by fifteen and nothing else, so a single division looks like the whole of the job.
wrong.move: writes one division from the fact and stops, as though a multiplication could be undone only one way.
wrong.screen: the fact card turns round on its own with the counters left exactly where they stand, and the rows are read the other way, thirteen rows of nine where there were nine rows of thirteen. A second blank division line opens under the child's first one, which stays written, and the new rows light one at a time while their count climbs at the top left.

wrong.why: twelve is the number written again and again down the working, so it is the number the eye keeps meeting, and the question's how many times is easy to hear as how many.
wrong.move: answers twelve when asked how many times twelve could be taken away from eighty-four.
wrong.screen: the takes are replayed from the tray one at a time, each take of twelve lifting off as one group and landing in a row along the bench, and the running count climbs by one for each take, not by twelve, until the tray is empty at seven. The child's twelve stays in the slot and the row of seven takes lies beside it, counted.

phases.screen: counters laid out in equal rows, with a fact card reading the multiplication above them

phases.does: deals the heap a round at a time, then drops each name tag on the thing it names
phases.goal: the dividend is shared by the divisor, the quotient is each share and the remainder is what is left

phases.feels: four names, four different things on the bench, and each tag has only one place to land

When too few are left to go round, move them into a saucer. Then write four cards reading dividend, divisor, quotient and remainder, and lay each card on the thing it names.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which number is being shared? Second rung, the phase's: into how many parts? Third rung: the bench is cut to a heap of nine on two plates, and the child tags all four numbers before the larger heap comes back. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: a division has a bigger number and a smaller one, and the answer to a sharing has always sounded like the small end of it.
wrong.move: calls six the quotient in seventy-nine shared among six, because it is the smaller of the two numbers in the story.
wrong.screen: the quotient tag is left lying where the child dropped it, on the plate dial, and the bench deals the seventy-nine a round at a time onto six plates: the round count at the top left climbs to thirteen and one plate's share reads thirteen underneath it. wrong.why: a counter on its own looks as if it belongs to somebody, and the plates are the only places on the bench that hold counters for anyone.
wrong.move: drops the remainder tag on one of the plates, because the leftover counter looks like one more share.
wrong.screen: the leftover counter is carried to that plate, which now holds fourteen while the other five hold thirteen, and the six plates are drawn plainly unequal side by side. The empty dish beside them lights, the counter walks back into it, and the plates settle level again with the child's tag still lying where it fell.

phases.screen: a heap in the tray, a row of plates, an empty leftover dish and four name tags at the side
phases.soWhat: The dividend is shared by the divisor, the quotient is each share, and the remainder is what is left.

phases.win: one more round leaves fewer in the dish than there are plates, and the check bar rebuilds the heap exactly
phases.does: tries to close the dish, deals one more round instead, then runs the check bar
phases.goal: the remainder is always smaller than the divisor, and divisor times quotient add remainder gives the dividend
phases.says: Look at the dish. Could every plate still take one more?
phases.check: Someone divides by five and says six are left over. Tell them what is wrong without working out the division.
phases.feels: a leftover as big as the plates is not a leftover yet, it is one more round waiting
phases.hands: Share fifty-eight counters among seven plates, but stop on purpose after seven rounds with nine still in the saucer. Ask whether the saucer could give every plate one more. Deal the extra round, count what is left, and then build the heap again: seven plates of eight, and add the two in the saucer.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many counters are in the dish? Second rung, the phase's: how many plates are there? Third rung: the bench is cut to eleven counters on three plates with the deal stopped after two rounds, and the child decides whether to deal again. Nothing already dealt is cleared.

wrong.why: the dealing has to stop somewhere, and a pile that is left looks like a leftover whatever its size.
wrong.move: stops dealing and writes the nine in the dish as the remainder, though seven of them could still go round.

The deal control lights, and one more round is dealt from the dish: each plate takes one, the dish is left holding two, and the lid closes by itself. The child's nine stays in the slot beside the new count, nothing marked.

wrong.why: the multiplication is the part that feels like the check, and the dish looks like something left out of the sum on purpose.
wrong.move: checks by multiplying the plates by the share and stops, without adding what is in the dish.
wrong.screen: the check bar builds the heap from the plates alone, seven rows of eight, and it stands beside the tray two counters short of the heap the tray began with. The two in the dish are then carried up and added, and the rebuilt heap matches the tray counter for counter. Both rebuilt heaps stay drawn.

phases.screen: a deal stopped early, with as many counters in the leftover dish as there are plates
phases.soWhat: The remainder is always smaller than the divisor, and divisor times quotient, add the remainder, gives back the dividend.

phases.win: three deals settle, and with no plates the deal never starts and the stage says there is nowhere to put a share
phases.does: deals onto one plate, then onto as many plates as counters, then empties the tray, then tries no plates
phases.goal: dividing by one leaves a number alone, a number other than zero divided by itself is one, and dividing by zero is not possible
phases.says: Try one plate. Now as many plates as counters. Now no plates at all.
phases.check: Fill these in: twenty-seven divided by one, and twenty-seven divided by twenty-seven. Then zero divided by twenty-seven, and twenty-seven divided by zero. Which one has no answer?
phases.feels: no plates is not a small number of plates, it is nowhere at all to put a share
phases.hands: Put twelve counters onto one plate, then share them onto twelve plates. Empty the tray and deal nothing onto four plates. Then take every plate away and ask the class to deal the twelve. Let them try, and ask where the first counter should go.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many plates has the dial set? Second rung, the phase's: where would the first counter go? Third rung: the bench is cut to a heap of three, dealt onto one plate, then three plates, then none, one after the other. The pad with its not possible key stays open.

wrong.why: zero divided by a number other than zero is zero, and the two sentences use the same two words the other way round.
wrong.move: says thirty-four divided by zero is zero, because with no plates nothing seems to be handed out.
wrong.screen: the dial is turned to none and the deal control stays unlit, the thirty-four counters staying in the tray exactly as they were. The caption says there is nowhere to put a share, no number is drawn anywhere on the stage for it, and the child's zero stays in the slot beside the pad's key reading not possible.

wrong.why: the rule was heard with the word always, and it gives one only when the number is other than zero; zero shared by zero looks exactly like a number shared by itself.
wrong.move: answers one for zero divided by zero, which has no answer, by reading it as a number divided by itself.
wrong.screen: the tray is emptied and the dial turned to none together, and the deal control stays unlit exactly as it did for thirty-four, because there are no plates and so nowhere to put a share, whatever the tray holds. The caption says this one is not possible too, the rule for a number and itself is lit with the words other than zero, and the child's one stays in the slot.

phases.screen: the same heap in the tray with the rule bay open beside the plate dial
phases.soWhat: Dividing by one leaves a number alone, a number other than zero divided by itself is one, and dividing by zero is not possible.

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment one more round is dealt from a dish that holds as many counters as there are plates. Every plate lights at once, one counter leaps from the dish to each plate in the same instant, and the dish is left holding fewer than the plates, so its lid swings shut by itself. The check bar then runs without being asked: the plates' shares stack into rows of ten beside the tray, the dish tips its last few in after them, and the rebuilt heap stands level with the tray, counter for counter. The round can be undone and dealt again as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the counters are laid out in equal rows under the fact card, the card reading the multiplication, and the two division lines under it stand blank. On the second a heap sits in the tray with the plates already set out by the dial, the leftover dish empty beside them and the four name tags lying at the side. On the third a deal stands stopped early, every plate holding the same, with as many counters in the dish as there are plates and the dish lid drawn open. On the fourth the same heap waits in the tray with the rule bay open beside the plate dial and the dial resting on one. The running count at the top left holds the rounds dealt against the counters in the heap, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the fact card, or the heap, or the open dish, or the dial, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks which number is being shared. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any heap up to ninety-nine counters and any number of plates, with the fact card, the name tags, the check bar and the rule bay all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.

observations.why: Equal rows can be read as rows of so many or as so many rows, and each reading divides by one of the two numbers that were multiplied.
observations.soWhat: Every multiplication fact with no zero in it hands over two division facts, and both of them should be written.
observations.observe: The fact card turned round and gave a second division without a single counter moving.

observations.why: The dividend is the heap, the divisor is how many plates, the quotient is one plate's share and the remainder is what sits in the dish.
observations.soWhat: The four names belong to four different things, so each one can be pointed at before it is written.
observations.observe: Every name tag settled on only one thing on the bench.

observations.why: That many counters could give every plate one more, so the sharing was not finished yet.
observations.soWhat: The remainder is always smaller than the divisor, and a bigger one means another round is due.
observations.observe: The dish would not close while it held as many counters as there were plates.

observations.why: Sharing needs somewhere to put each share, and with no plates there is nowhere at all.
observations.soWhat: Dividing by zero is not possible for any number, so zero divided by zero is not possible either.
observations.observe: With no plates the deal never started, and no number appeared anywhere on the stage.

source_tool.description: A bench runs across the stage with a heap of counters in a tray at the left and a row of plates along the middle. A dial sets how many plates there are. Dealing is done a round at a time, one counter onto every plate, and each round lifts exactly as many counters out of the tray as there are plates, so the rounds are the repeated taking away the recap asks for, drawn rather than written. A round counter at the top left of the canvas keeps the number of rounds, which is the share on each plate. When too few counters are left to go round, they are set down in a leftover dish beside the plates at full strength, and the dish refuses to close while it holds as many as there are plates, lighting every plate that could still take one more. Four name tags wait at the side, dividend, divisor, quotient and remainder, to be dropped on the heap, the plate dial, one plate's share and the dish. A fact card above the bench turns a picture of equal rows round, so one multiplication is read as two divisions. A check bar under the plates multiplies the plates by the share, adds the dish, and rebuilds the heap beside the tray. A rule bay sets the dial to one plate, to as many plates as counters and to no plates at all, and empties the tray for a deal of nothing. With no plates the deal will not start, and the stage says there is nowhere to put a share rather than showing any number.
source_tool.art_direction: Counters dealt onto a row of plates / Picture book

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a tray of counters and a row of plates, digit cards under place headings, sticks tied in bundles, a long division frame with its bracket, a ladder of multiples, a strip of cells, a story card, and two rails tied at every stop.

Equal shares are drawn genuinely equal and genuinely countable. Where a plate or a part is labelled with a number, exactly that many things are on it, and anything counted one at a time is drawn in rows of ten so that no more than twenty loose things ever have to be counted singly.

What is left over is drawn OUTSIDE the shares, in a dish or a slot of its own, at full strength and fully countable. It is never faded, never tucked under a share and never left to be guessed from a gap.
A division is always written with every place headed. The number being divided at a step is shown with its place name, so fifteen tens is never drawn as a bare fifteen.

Every zero in a quotient is drawn at the same size and weight as the other digits and is never dimmed, shrunk or dropped. A zero is written only where the number being divided is smaller than the divisor, and a leading zero may stand or be left off, but a zero after the first digit always stands.
What is left at every step is drawn in its own slot before the next digit comes down, and it slides down to join that digit so the next number can be seen being made.
A remainder is written as a number. A zero standing in front of its other digits is lifted off and set aside, never written into the answer.
No stage ever shows a number for a division by zero. Where one is asked, the stage says it is not possible and draws nothing to share into.
Two answers being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one beside or above the other. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a counter, a digit or a card the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The dividend, the whole being shared and any total, is deep blue; the divisor, and the plates, groups or envelopes it makes, is amber; the quotient and each equal share are green; and what is left over, at one step or at the end, is vermilion. Those four hold from the plates to the frame to the story card in every tool of this chapter. A multiple of the divisor, whether it is being tried on the ladder or taken away as a chunk, is rose, so the chunks can be added up without being mistaken for the share. A zero written in the quotient because the number was smaller than the divisor is grey, and grey never means faint: it is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit, because it is holding a place. All of that holds in greyscale, because what is left over is told apart by the dish or the left slot it sits in, and a quotient digit by the row it sits in, before either is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.

phase_map.concept: Dividing by one, by itself and by zero

placement.where: Straight after a heap of real counters has been shared onto paper plates by hand, and before any division has been written down. The tool is what refuses to close a sharing while the leftover could still go round once more, and what will not start a deal onto no plates at all, which a heap of counters on a desk cannot refuse.

answer_key.rule: Division is equal sharing or equal grouping. The number being shared is the dividend, the number of equal parts is the divisor, the size of each part is the quotient, and anything left over is the remainder. The remainder is always smaller than the divisor, because as many as the divisor would give every part one more. Divisor times quotient, add the remainder, gives back the dividend. A division that leaves nothing over is sometimes called a perfect division, and that is all the phrase means: nothing left over. A multiplication fact with no zero in it gives two division facts, one for each number that was multiplied. Dividing by one leaves a number as it is. A number other than zero divided by itself is one. Zero divided by a number other than zero is zero. Dividing by zero is not possible, for every number, zero included.
answer_key.wrong: The deal is run again a round at a time with the rounds counted aloud, the leftover dish is emptied back onto the plates while it can still go round, and the check bar rebuilds the heap. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The product, 117, is the number being divided in both facts.
Dividing by one of the two numbers that were multiplied gives back the other: 117 divided by 13 is 9.
Dividing by the other gives back the first: 117 divided by 9 is 13.
items.answer: 117 divided by 13 is 9, and 117 divided by 9 is 13
items.question: 9 times 13 is 117. Write the two division facts this one multiplication gives.
items.checkpoint: A multiplication fact with no zero in it gives two division facts, one for each number that was multiplied.
items.misconception: Writing only one of the two facts, as if a multiplication could be undone in only one way.

steps: 79 is the number being shared, so it is the dividend, and the 6 bags make 6 the divisor.
Each round puts one marble in every bag and uses 6, and thirteen rounds use 78.
One marble is left and cannot go round all 6 bags, so the quotient is 13 and the remainder is 1.
items.answer: The dividend is 79, the divisor is 6, the quotient is 13 and the remainder is 1
items.question: 79 marbles are shared equally among 6 bags. Name the dividend, the divisor, the quotient and the remainder.
items.checkpoint: The dividend is shared, the divisor says into how many, the quotient is each share, and the remainder is what is left.
items.misconception: Calling 6 the quotient because it is the smaller of the two numbers in the story.

steps: 7 friends with 7 stickers each uses 49, which leaves 9.
9 is not smaller than 7, so one more round can be dealt: 8 each uses 56 and leaves 2.
Check: 7 times 8 is 56, and 56 add 2 is 58, the dividend.
items.answer: 9 left over is too many, because 7 of them could give every friend one more. The answer is 8 each, with 2 left over
items.question: A child shares 58 stickers among 7 friends, gives 7 each, and says 9 are left over. What went wrong, and what is the right answer?
items.checkpoint: The remainder is always smaller than the divisor, and divisor times quotient, add the remainder, gives back the dividend.
items.misconception: Stopping the sharing while the leftover pile is still as big as the divisor.

steps: All 34 things on one plate leave 34 on it, so dividing by one leaves a number as it is.
34 things on 34 plates put one on each, and with nothing to share, 34 plates get 0 each.
With no plates at all there is nowhere to put a share, so dividing by zero is not possible.
items.answer: 34 divided by 1 is 34, 34 divided by 34 is 1, 0 divided by 34 is 0, and 34 divided by 0 is not possible
items.question: Work out 34 divided by 1, 34 divided by 34, and 0 divided by 34. Then say what 34 divided by 0 is.
items.checkpoint: A number other than zero divided by itself is one, zero divided by a number other than zero is zero, and dividing by zero is not possible.
items.misconception: Saying a number divided by zero is zero, or is the number itself, because nothing seems to have been done to it.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: 6 times 17 is 102. Write both division facts it gives.
items.final_answer: 102 divided by 17 is 6, and 102 divided by 6 is 17

items.question: Take 12 away from 84 again and again until nothing is left. How many times did you take it away, and what division does that show?
items.final_answer: 7 times, which shows that 84 divided by 12 is 7

items.question: In 95 divided by 8, which number is the dividend and which is the divisor?
items.final_answer: 95 is the dividend and 8 is the divisor

items.question: 65 seeds are planted equally in 4 pots. Find the quotient and the remainder, and say what each one means.
items.final_answer: The quotient is 16, the seeds in each pot, and the remainder is 1, the seed left over

items.question: Find the quotient and remainder of 71 divided by 9, and check the answer by multiplying back.
items.final_answer: 7 remainder 8, and 9 times 7 is 63, add 8 makes 71

items.question: A child divides a number by 5 and says the remainder is 6. How do you know straight away that this is wrong?
items.final_answer: The remainder must be smaller than the divisor, and 6 is not smaller than 5, so one more 5 could still be shared out

items.question: Fill in the blanks: 527 divided by 1 is ___, 527 divided by 527 is ___, 0 divided by 527 is ___, and 527 divided by 0 is ___.
items.final_answer: 527, then 1, then 0, and the last is not possible

items.question: Is zero divided by zero equal to one, to zero, or not possible? Say which rule decides it.
items.final_answer: Not possible. Dividing by zero is not possible for any number, zero included. The rules that give one and zero hold only when the divisor is other than zero

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: sets how many plates the heap is shared onto, from none upwards
puts one counter on every plate and lifts that many out of the tray
keeps the number of rounds dealt, which is the share on each plate
holds what cannot go round, and will not close while every plate could take one more
dividend, divisor, quotient and remainder, each dropped on the thing it names
turns a picture of equal rows round, so one multiplication reads as two divisions
multiplies the plates by the share and adds the dish to rebuild the heap
sets one plate, as many plates as counters, an empty tray, or no plates at all

teaching_notes: Share a real heap onto paper plates before the tool is opened, one counter to each plate a round at a time, and count the rounds out loud. Each round takes away as many counters as there are plates, which is the repeated taking away the recap asks for, and the number of rounds is the share on each plate. Then use the tool for the two things a desk cannot do. It will not let a sharing stop while the leftover could still go round once more, which is why the remainder is always smaller than the divisor. And it will not start a deal onto no plates at all. The chapter states its rule for a number divided by itself, and its rule for zero divided by a number, with the word always and no condition. Zero divided by zero meets all three of its rules and would get three answers: one, zero and not possible. Only the last is right, so say each rule for a divisor other than zero, and if a child asks about zero divided by zero, the answer is that it is not possible, like every division by zero. The recap's worked model turns six fifteens into ninety divided by fifteen, and three of its items divide by the other number, so show both division facts from every multiplication rather than letting the model look like the only way. The summary box calls a division that comes out whole a perfect division. Every division in the chapter has a whole number quotient, so say what is meant: nothing left over. The six highlighted words make a set of flashcards, and four of them are the name tags on this bench.
generation_prompt: Build a sharing tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A tray of countable counters sits at the left of the working area, drawn in rows of ten so a heap of up to ninety-nine can be read at a glance, with a row of round plates along the middle and a leftover dish beside them. A plate dial sets the number of plates, from none upwards. A deal control puts one counter on every plate at once and lifts exactly that many out of the tray, and a round counter at the top left of the canvas records each round, because the rounds are the share on each plate. When fewer counters remain than there are plates, they move into the leftover dish at full strength and stay countable. The dish refuses to close while it holds as many counters as there are plates: every plate that could take one more lights, and nothing is marked. Four name tags reading dividend, divisor, quotient and remainder wait at the side and settle only on the heap, the dial, one plate's share and the dish. A fact card above the bench shows the same counters as equal rows and turns them round, writing one division for each reading. A check bar under the plates multiplies the plates by the share, adds the dish and rebuilds the heap beside the tray. A rule bay sets one plate, as many plates as counters, an empty tray, and no plates at all; with no plates the deal control stays unlit, the caption says there is nowhere to put a share, and no number is ever shown for it. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Deal one counter to every plate, a round at a time. Count the rounds. Put what cannot go round in the dish. Drop each name tag on what it names. Then try one plate, and no plates at all.
